chunks.section: An Analytical Model of Compute-limited Multistage Training Pipelines
chunks.text: Nishil Patel Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit Affiliation: University College London Email: nishil.patel@ucl.ac.uk Jin Hwa Lee Affiliation: Sainsbury Wellcome Centre Affiliation: University College London Basile Confavreux Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit Affiliation: University College London Andrew Saxe Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit Affiliation: Sainsbury Wellcome Centre Affiliation: University College London

chunks.section: Abstract
chunks.text: Modern foundation models are trained through multiple stages, yet how these stages interact and how compute should be allocated across them remain poorly understood. We introduce an analytically tractable high-dimensional model combining unsupervised pretraining with a linear autoencoder, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with noisy stepwise labels, and reinforcement learning (RL) with sparse episodic rewards. Using random matrix theory and an operator-projection closure, we derive approximate low-dimensional learning dynamics that closely match simulations. We show that finite pretraining data imposes a representation-dependent performance limit, with Bayes classification error scaling as the inverse square root of the pretraining sample ratio, and observe the same exponent in asymptotic SFT and RL errors. Better pretraining also reduces sensitivity to noisy supervision. SFT initialization shortens the initial RL plateau induced by sparse rewards, an effect we also observe in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Optimizing compute across all three stages reveals that the optimal allocation depends on supervision quality and total budget, with a non-monotonic dependence of the RL compute share on budget. Finally, a complementary compositional model shows how RL selectively strengthens task-relevant pretrained skills while largely preserving unused skills. Together, these results identify mechanisms linking representation quality, feedback structure, and compute allocation in multistage training.

chunks.section: 1 Introduction
chunks.text: Modern foundation models exhibit transformative capabilities from human-level language comprehension and production Radford et al. (2019) ; Brown et al. (2020) ; Touvron et al. (2023) , to reasoning across modalities and mathematical problem-solving Jaech et al. (2024) ; Shao et al. (2024) ; Chervonyi et al. (2025) ; Team et al. (2025) . Multistage training is a critical aspect of the training paradigm of such models, which consists of unsupervised auto-regressive pretraining followed by several stages of supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning on smaller, domain-specific datasets Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Achiam et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025) . Yet, the consequences of different training stages and their interactions remain poorly understood. Empirical investigation of these questions is difficult, as it requires substantial compute and costly human annotation, constraining the scope of hypotheses that can be explored Zhao et al. (2025) ; Shao et al. (2025) ; Akter et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025a) .

chunks.section: 1 Introduction
chunks.text: Alongside the transition to multistage training pipelines, foundation models reflect a second shift from a sample-complexity–centric view of learning to a compute-centric one. Whereas classical theory treats data as the limiting resource and implicitly assumes unbounded compute, modern foundation models invert this assumption: data is abundant, compute is limited, and performance scales predictably with model size and training compute, as evidenced by large-scale empirical scaling laws Kaplan et al. (2020) ; Hoffmann et al. (2022) . In this compute-limited regime, models are rarely trained to convergence, and performance is instead determined by how a fixed computational budget is allocated across model capacity and multiple training stages. Together, these two shifts—toward multistage pipelines and the compute-limited regime—pose a challenge for existing theory, which offers limited guidance for analyzing learning dynamics, performance trade-offs, or compute allocation in modern foundation model training. —

chunks.section: Contributions.
chunks.text: —To this end, we develop an analytically tractable high-dimensional model based on statistical physics Seung et al. (1992) ; Saad and Solla (1995) ; Zdeborová and Krzakala (2016) . The model isolates the effects of pretrained representation quality, dense stepwise supervision, and sparse episodic rewards. We derive deterministic learning dynamics in the high-dimensional limit and obtain a tractable, approximately closed system of ODEs, allowing us to study how pretrained representations, supervision quality, and compute allocation jointly determine downstream performance. Our contributions are: • We combine random matrix theory with an operator-projection closure to obtain a low-dimensional approximation of the SFT and RL dynamics, validated against simulations. We derive the α − 1 / 2 \alpha^{-1/2} scaling of the representation-dependent Bayes error with pretraining sample size and observe the same exponent in asymptotic finetuning error. • We characterize how SFT and RL complement each other. SFT shortens the initial sparse-reward plateau, an effect also observed in OLMo-2 1B on GSM8K. Under spherical normalization and locally optimal learning rates, longer SFT warm starts additionally improve asymptotic RL performance. Better pretraining also reduces the excess SFT error caused by label noise. • We optimize compute allocation across pretraining, SFT, and RL. The optimal split depends on both supervision quality and the total budget: noisier labels favour RL, while the optimal RL share can vary non-monotonically with total compute. • We extend the model to compositional tasks, showing how prior skill proficiency accelerates RL and how finetuning selectively improves task-relevant skills while largely preserving unused skills.

chunks.section: Empirical interactions
chunks.text: across training stages. Controlled studies have investigated how pretraining shapes the effectiveness of downstream reinforcement learning. Shen et al. (2026) examine a complete pretraining-–SFT-–RL pipeline and relate pretraining loss and data scale to post-RL performance and learning speed, including a pretraining–-RL compute frontier. Zhang et al. (2026a) isolate the effects of pretraining, intermediate training, and RL on compositional reasoning tasks. Zhao et al. (2024) investigate the amplification of pretrained behaviors under RL. Empirical work compares the generalization behavior of SFT and outcome-based RL ( Chu et al., 2025 ) and demonstrates that higher standalone SFT accuracy need not yield better subsequent RL performance ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Kang et al., 2026 ) .

chunks.section: Closure of structured-data learning dynamics.
chunks.text: The problem of anisotropic data covariance generating an infinite hierarchy of order parameters has been studied in the context of online learning with structured data Yoshida and Okada (2019) . In that work, the authors show that the ODE system can only be closed if the covariance has a finite number of unique eigenvalues, where there is a pair of order parameters associated to every unique eigenvalue. There are several works that address this feature: approaches include replacing the infinite discrete hierarchy by a closed functional object — a spectral order parameter ( Goldt et al., 2020 ; Goldt et al., 2022 ) or a resolvent ( Collins-Woodfin et al., 2024 ) . However, this is non-trivial to implement in the case of a random data covariance. Another more recent approach most similar in spirit to ours is Xu et al. (2026) , where the authors show the infinite hierarchy can be exponentially well approximated by a finite truncated system. Ours is merely a different method of truncation, without a proof of exponential convergence.

chunks.section: Pretraining
chunks.text: We draw a fixed pretraining dataset 𝐗 ∈ ℝ N × D \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} with independent rows distributed as 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝚺 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}) , where 𝚺 = 𝐌 s + Δ ​ 𝐌 n \mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathbf{M}_{s}+\Delta\mathbf{M}_{n} , 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{s} projects onto a signal subspace of dimension ρ ​ D \rho D , and 𝐌 n = 𝐈 − 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{n}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{M}_{s} . We take 0 < ρ < 1 0<\rho<1 , 0 < Δ < 1 0<\Delta<1 , and the high-dimensional limit N , D → ∞ N,D\to\infty at fixed α = N / D > ρ \alpha=N/D>\rho . A linear autoencoder (LAE) with hidden width ρ ​ D \rho D learns the empirical principal subspace of this dataset when trained to convergence ( Baldi and Hornik, 1989 ; Saxe et al., 2019 ) . We represent its learned subspace by the orthogonal projector 𝐏 \mathbf{P} . Downstream observations are 𝐱 ~ = 𝐏𝐱 \tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{x} , with fresh 𝐱 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝚺 ) \mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}) . 𝐏 \mathbf{P} remains fixed throughout finetuning. Thus α \alpha determines how much task-relevant signal is available for the downstream task. The LAE learns a compressed feature subspace from unlabelled data, abstracting the role of pretraining as representation learning: discovering reusable structure and organizing inputs into a feature space ( Bengio et al., 2012 ; LeCun et al., 2015 ; LeCun and others, 2022 ; Bommasani et al., 2021 ) . This frozen-feature assumption is motivated by evidence that finetuning preserves pretrained representations ( Nadipalli, 2025 ) and the success of PEFT ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Han et al., 2024 )

chunks.text: The finetuning task is organized in episodes of length T T , where a student perceptron 𝐰 ∈ Range ⁡ ( 𝐏 ) \mathbf{w}\in\mathrm{Range}(\mathbf{P}) makes a series of binary decisions y t = sgn ​ ( 𝐱 ~ 𝐭 ⊺ ​ 𝐰 D ) y_{t}=\text{sgn}\left(\frac{\mathbf{\tilde{x}_{t}}^{\intercal}\mathbf{w}}{\sqrt{D}}\right) given the raw observations 𝐱 1 ​ … ​ T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝚺 ) \mathbf{x}_{1\dots T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{\Sigma}) projected onto the encoder subspace by 𝐏 \mathbf{P} . Data labels for supervision/reward y t ∗ = sgn ​ ( 𝐱 ⊺ ​ 𝐰 ∗ D ) y_{t}^{*}=\text{sgn}\left(\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\intercal}\mathbf{w^{*}}}{\sqrt{D}}\right) are specified by a teacher perceptron 𝐰 ∗ ∈ R D \mathbf{w}^{*}\in R^{D} , which has access to the raw data 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , importantly, it sees the entire signal subspace. The teacher is a fixed-weight oracle that generates the target labels. During SFT and RL, the weights of the student are updated with feedback from the teacher, but the core difference lies in how the feedback from the output is given to the student. This setting is inspired by the teacher–student framework ( Gardner and Derrida, 1989 ; Seung et al., 1992 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1993 ) . We discuss related teacher–student models in Appendix .1 .

chunks.section: SFT:
chunks.text: Each individual sample in the episode contributes separately to the update by error feedback with the corresponding teacher label ( Figure 1 a, pink box). The update follows the Perceptron rule ( Rosenblatt, 1958 ) . The update at the μ th \mu_{\text{th}} episode can be written as 𝐰 ( μ + 1 ) = 𝐰 ( μ ) − η T ​ D ​ ∑ t = 1 T y t ( μ ) ​ 𝐱 ~ t ( μ ) ​ θ ​ ( − y SFT ∗ t ( μ ) ​ y t ( μ ) ) , \displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{(\mu+1)}=\mathbf{w}^{(\mu)}-\frac{\eta}{T\sqrt{D}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}y_{t}^{(\mu)}\mathbf{\tilde{x}}_{t}^{(\mu)}\theta(-{y^{*}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}_{t}^{(\mu)}y_{t}^{(\mu)}), (1) where θ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \theta(\cdot) is the heaviside step function and η \eta is the learning rate. This can be interpreted as the linearized gradient descent update on the mean squared loss Σ t = 1 T ​ ( y t − y SFT ∗ t ) 2 \Sigma_{t=1}^{T}(y_{t}-{y^{*}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}_{t})^{2} . The teacher labels for SFT are generated with noise, i.e. y SFT ∗ t = y t ∗ ​ z t {y^{*}_{\mathrm{SFT}}}_{t}=y^{*}_{t}z_{t} , where z t z_{t} takes the values of 1 or -1 with probability ( 1 − ϵ ) (1-\epsilon) or ϵ \epsilon respectively. This is a simple model of imperfect supervision, which is common in real-world datasets. N.B. this label noise is unique to SFT in our model. Importantly, the student receives an individual update for every t t . For example, in multi-step math tasks, this is equivalent to getting a supervised learning signal at every step of a solution.

chunks.section: RL:
chunks.text: We use the RL perceptron update of Patel et al. (2025) , which extends the teacher-student framework to online policy learning under a sequential decision-making task. Given the same finetuning task, the critical difference with SFT lies in the bulk feedback: the student is updated using a delayed, sparse reward signal at the end of the episode, rather than at every step, as in SFT. The update at μ th \mu_{\text{th}} episode can be written as 𝐰 ( μ + 1 ) = 𝐰 ( μ ) + η T ( ∑ t = 1 T y t ( μ ) ​ 𝐱 ~ t ( μ ) D ) R ( y 1 : T ( μ ) , y ∗ 1 : T ( μ ) ) , \displaystyle\mathbf{w}^{(\mu+1)}=\mathbf{w}^{(\mu)}+\frac{\eta}{T}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{y_{t}^{(\mu)}\mathbf{\tilde{x}}_{t}^{(\mu)}}{\sqrt{D}}\right)R(y_{1:T}^{(\mu)},{y^{*}}^{(\mu)}_{1:T}), (2)

chunks.section: RL:
chunks.text: where the reward rule is specified by R ( y 1 : T , y 1 : T ∗ ) R(y_{1:T},y^{*}_{1:T}) . In this work, we mainly use the reward condition, every action in an episode must be correct , (i.e y t = y ∗ t , ∀ t ∈ 1 , … T y_{t}=y^{*}_{t},~\forall t\in 1,\dots T , or R = Π t = 1 T ​ θ ​ ( y t ​ y t ∗ ) R=\Pi_{t=1}^{T}\theta(y_{t}y_{t}^{*}) ). This is akin to RLVR where reward is received based on the correctness of a final result, where the final result requires multiple previous steps to be correct in order to reach it. The episode length T T controls the difficulty of the task. Larger values of T T make the task more difficult as the model needs to make a longer sequence of correct decisions, giving an idealized analogue of verifiable-reward methods such as GRPO ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) . This task structure reflects the nature of multi-step problems, for example, a math problem requiring multiple steps of reasoning to be correct. When we consider multiple stages of finetuning (e.g. SFT followed by RL), each stage trains the same student and uses the final student state of the previous stage as the initial student state of the subsequent stage. We use it not as a literal model of full finetuning, but to isolate how representation quality constrains later learning.

chunks.section: 4.1 Closing the ODEs
chunks.text: Evaluating the expectations in Equations 4 and 5 introduces higher-order products of the pretraining and signal/noise projectors, such as 𝐔 i ​ j = 𝐏𝐌 i ​ 𝐏𝐌 j ​ 𝐏 \mathbf{U}_{ij}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{i}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{j}\mathbf{P} . Their associated order parameters in turn depend on higher-order products, generating a hierarchy of dynamical observables. We truncate this hierarchy by approximating higher-order operators through projection onto the retained lower-order operator basis. This is a polynomial least-squares approximation and can be applied at any chosen truncation order. Here, we retain the four order parameters ( J s , J n , Q s , Q n ) (J_{s},J_{n},Q_{s},Q_{n}) , using 𝐔 i ​ j ≈ Ω i ​ j ( s ) ​ 𝐏𝐌 s ​ 𝐏 + Ω i ​ j ( n ) ​ 𝐏𝐌 n ​ 𝐏 , \mathbf{U}_{ij}\approx\Omega_{ij}^{(s)}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{s}\mathbf{P}+\Omega_{ij}^{(n)}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{n}\mathbf{P}, with coefficients chosen to minimize the squared Frobenius norm of the operator approximation error. A six-order-parameter closure is considered in the appendix. The projection coefficients are completely determined by normalized trace moments m k = 1 D ​ Tr ⁡ [ ( 𝐏𝐌 s ) k ] . m_{k}=\frac{1}{D}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{s})^{k}\bigr]. For the four-order-parameter closure, only m 1 m_{1} , m 2 m_{2} , and m 3 m_{3} are required. Random matrix theory determines the exact high-dimensional limits of these moments, which agree with empirical PCA and trained-LAE measurements in Figure 2 a. The resulting dynamical closure remains approximate because it truncates the order-parameter hierarchy. The derivation and random-matrix calculations are given in Appendices A and B . We empirically assess accuracy of the higher order closure in Section A.6 .

chunks.section: 5 Results
chunks.text: We examine how pretraining sample size α = N / D \alpha=N/D and SFT label noise ϵ \epsilon affect learning dynamics, asymptotic performance, and the benefit of SFT before RL. We then optimize compute allocation across the three training stages and extend the model to study how RL modifies individual skills in compositional tasks.

chunks.section: SFT and RL exhibit distinct learning dynamics.
chunks.text: The closed ODEs closely match simulated order-parameter trajectories for both SFT and RL ( Figure 2 b–c). SFT begins learning immediately from stepwise supervision, whereas RL exhibits an initial plateau followed by rapid improvement. Under the all-correct reward criterion, an episode produces an update with probability P T P^{T} . Rewards are therefore rare when initial accuracy is low, but become more frequent as learning progresses. This accounts for the longer plateaus at larger episode lengths T T reported in Patel et al. (2025) . Figure 2 d shows accuracy throughout SFT followed by RL, when the pretraining level and time durations of SFT/RL are jointly optimized for different total compute budgets. We examine the benefits of SFT initialization below and the allocation problem in Section 5.1 . Unless otherwise stated, subsequent experiments use a locally optimal learning rate η opt \eta_{\mathrm{opt}} that maximizes the instantaneous predicted increase in generalization accuracy (see Section A.9 ).

chunks.section: SFT and RL attain the Bayes scaling exponent.
chunks.text: Figure 3 a shows that the asymptotic SFT and RL errors decrease as α − 1 / 2 \alpha^{-1/2} , matching the scaling of the representation-dependent Bayes error despite remaining above it. For an isotropic teacher in the signal subspace, at large α \alpha , Appendix C gives e B ( α ) = Δ ​ 1 − ρ π ⁡ ( 1 − Δ ) α − 1 / 2 + O ( α − 1 ) . e_{B}(\alpha)=\frac{\Delta\sqrt{1-\rho}}{\pi(1-\Delta)}\alpha^{-1/2}+O(\alpha^{-1}). This result identifies a mechanism by which increasing pretraining data produces power-law improvements in downstream performance. The α − 1 / 2 \alpha^{-1/2} scaling follows from the accuracy of the pretrained subspace: finite-sample covariance fluctuations leave an unrecoverable fraction of teacher-field variance of order α − 1 \alpha^{-1} , and the Bayes classification error scales as the square root of this fraction.

chunks.section: SFT warm starts improve asymptotic RL performance.
chunks.text: Under the spherical constraint and locally optimal learning rate used in Figure 3 a–b, increasing the duration of SFT reduces the asymptotic error of subsequent RL. Figure 3 b reports e RL ∞ ​ ( ξ SFT ) − e RL ∞ ​ ( ∞ ) e_{\rm RL}^{\infty}(\xi_{\rm SFT})-e_{\rm RL}^{\infty}(\infty) , the excess error relative to RL initialized from converged SFT. For short warm starts, this excess error depends strongly on pretraining quality. At longer SFT durations, the curves approach a common power-law decay, indicating similar convergence towards their respective fully warm-started RL asymptotes.

chunks.section: Reward stringency mediates a speed accuracy tradeoff.
chunks.text: We consider the reward function that rewards an episode when at least n n of its T T decisions are correct, R = 𝟏 ​ ( ∑ t = 1 T θ ⁡ ( y t ​ y t ∗ ) ≥ n ) R=\mathbf{1}(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\theta(y_{t}y_{t}^{*})\geq n) . As noted by Patel et al. (2025) , Figure 3 d shows that relaxing the all-correct criterion can accelerate early learning at the expense of asymptotic accuracy. With constant learning rate and unconstrained weights, the initial accuracy slope is larger by a factor ( T − 1 n − 1 ) \binom{T-1}{n-1} than under the all-correct rule. However, the asymptotic error decays as e g ( ξ ) ∝ ( log ξ ) − 1 / ( T − n ) e_{g}(\xi)\propto(\log\xi)^{-1/(T-n)} for n < T n<T , compared with e g ​ ( ξ ) ∝ log ⁡ ξ / ξ e_{g}(\xi)\propto\sqrt{\log\xi/\xi} for n = T n=T . Less stringent reward therefore allows faster initial learning but slower asymptotic convergence. Intuitively, this is because early in learning rewards are more frequent with less stringent reward, but conversely near convergence episodes containing incorrect decisions are increasingly rewarded. With spherical normalization and constant learning rate, the small-error stationary solution instead scales as e g ∞ ∝ ( η / Q ) 1 / ( T − n + 2 ) e_{g}^{\infty}\propto(\eta/Q)^{1/(T-n+2)} as η / Q → 0 \eta/Q\to 0 , where Q = Q s + Q n Q=Q_{s}+Q_{n} is fixed. The derivations are provided in Section E.2 .

chunks.section: SFT overcomes the RL plateau.
chunks.text: Figure 4 a compares RL trajectories initialized after different amounts of SFT. Increasing the duration of preceding SFT raises the initial probability of a successful episode to a higher degree, allowing subsequent RL to quickly improve performance. A corresponding qualitative effect appears in OLMo-2 1B ( for AI (Ai2) et al., 2025 ) finetuned on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021a ) ( Figure 4 b): models initialized from SFT checkpoints show faster reward improvement while the RL-only baseline initially remains near zero. Experimental details are in Appendix J . We next include the costs of all stages to evaluate the complete pipeline. Figure 4 : SFT overcomes the RL Plateau. (a) Pure RL exhibits a plateau due to reward sparsity (yellow). It is beneficial to first run SFT to overcome this plateau (navy) since SFT provides dense supervision without waiting for a successful episode. (b) We replicate that early SFT complementing RL by removing plateau in a realistic model and task using OlMo2 1B ( OLMo et al., 2024 ) and GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021b ) . chunks.section: 5.1 Optimal compute budget allocation
chunks.text: The previous section showed that fine-tuning performance is shaped by both the quality of the pretrained representation and the reliability of SFT supervision. We therefore extend our compute-allocation analysis to the full training pipeline, including pretraining, and ask how the optimal allocation changes as the SFT data quality varies. The compute costs for SFT and RL are computed as defined in Section F.1 .

chunks.section: Compute model and allocation objective.
chunks.text: We count a multiply-add as two FLOPs. For an LAE of hidden width ρ ​ D \rho D , trained for M M updates on a fixed batch of size α ​ D \alpha D , the assigned pretraining cost is C PT = 10 ​ M ​ α ​ ρ ​ D 3 C_{\rm PT}=10M\alpha\rho D^{3} . The assigned SFT and RL cost per episode is c ep = 2 ​ ρ ​ T ​ D 2 c_{\rm ep}=2\rho TD^{2} , including the frozen encoder projection and readout update. Thus a finetuning duration ξ \xi costs D ​ c ep ​ ξ Dc_{\rm ep}\xi when ξ = μ / D \xi=\mu/D . The resulting budget constraint is 2 ​ ρ ​ D 3 ​ ( 5 ​ M ​ α + T ⁡ ( ξ SFT + ξ RL ) ) ≤ B FLOPs . 2\rho D^{3}(5M\alpha+T(\xi_{\rm SFT}+\xi_{\rm RL}))\leq\mathrm{B}_{\rm FLOPs}. For convenience, we express compute in normalized units, B ~ = B FLOPs / ( 2 ​ ρ ​ D 3 ) \widetilde{B}=B_{\rm FLOPs}/(2\rho D^{3}) , so that the budget constraint becomes 5 ​ M ​ α + T ⁡ ( ξ SFT + ξ RL ) ≤ B ~ . 5M\alpha+T(\xi_{\rm SFT}+\xi_{\rm RL})\leq\widetilde{B}. All compute budgets reported in the following figures are in these normalized units unless otherwise stated. We numerically optimize the final accuracy over the pretraining level and the SFT/RL durations, with SFT preceding RL. Costs and optimization details are given in Sections F.1 and H .

chunks.section: Pretraining quality and budget determine the optimal SFT–RL split.
chunks.text: Figure 5 c shows the optimal fraction of finetuning compute allocated to RL at fixed pretraining level α \alpha . At a given budget, better pretraining increases the optimal RL fraction, whereas at fixed α \alpha , increasing the finetuning budget shifts the optimal allocation towards SFT. The optimality of increasing the proportion of preceding SFT compute is consistent with the warm-start dependence in Figure 3 b: longer SFT can improve the asymptotic performance of subsequent RL, in addition to shortening its initial plateau.

chunks.section: Optimal budget allocation under varying conditions
chunks.text: When compute is allocated jointly across all three stages, pretraining receives the largest share ( Figure 5 a–b). The optimal RL share initially increases with the total budget before decreasing ( Figure 5 a), demonstrating that additional compute need not favour a progressively larger RL allocation. Within the remaining fine-tuning budget, SFT remains important at low noise because it helps overcome the initial RL plateau through dense supervision ( Figure 5 a). At a fixed total budget, increasing intermediate-label noise increases the optimal RL share in Figure 5 b. Intuitively, at zero label noise, SFT is compute optimal, and increasing noise reduces its effectiveness. In Figure 5 d, we compare the maximum achievable performance under three training paradigms: the full pretraining + SFT + RL pipeline (blue), pretraining + SFT only (green), and pretraining + RL only (pink). The full three-stage pipeline is compute-optimal the entire compute-limited regime, showing the benefit of combining SFT and RL as we demonstrated previously by showing SFT removes the early reward plateau from RL. At smaller compute budgets, SFT-only outperforms RL-only, and is compute optimal in the multi-stage case too, since it can overcome the RL plateau. But as compute budgets increase, the optimality of RL-only surpasses the SFT-only, since it avoids noisy SFT supervision. However, it still falls short of the full three-stage pipeline, due the increase in asymptotic performance afforded by SFT warm-start.

chunks.section: 5.2 RL finetuning and skill amplification
chunks.text: So far, we have treated pretraining quality as a single scalar controlling the overall usefulness of the learned representation. In practice, however, pretrained models may contain many latent skills, only some of which are relevant to a given downstream task. Fine-tuning on a domain specific task, such as on math or coding, may therefore selectively amplify task-relevant skills rather than uniformly improve the full representation Zhao et al. (2025) ; Shao et al. (2025) . This motivates the question: how does the fine-tuning task specification influence the skills acquired during pretraining? We address this question by extending our analytical model to study RL finetuning as learning to linearly compose multiple ‘pretrained’ skills into a more complex task ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Concretely, each skill is represented by one of K K independent teacher-student pairs ( 𝐰 1 ​ … ​ K ∗ , 𝐰 1 ​ … ​ K \mathbf{w}^{*}_{1...K},\mathbf{w}_{1...K} ), and the downstream task is defined by a context teacher-student vector ( V ∗ , V ∈ ℝ K V^{*},V\in\mathbb{R}^{K} ) that selects and combines these skills. During fine-tuning, both the student skills and the context are updated. This setup allows some pretrained skills to be task-relevant, while others are present in the base model but unused by the downstream task. We provide the ODE derivation for this compositional RL setting in Appendix I . The notion of pretraining in this setup is how well each skill is learned before the downstream task.

chunks.section: Prior skill proficiency accelerates relevant RL finetuning.
chunks.text: We first vary the initial proficiency of each skill and measure the fine-tuning time required to reach 99% of the maximal task performance. Fine-tuning converges exponentially faster as prior skill proficiency improves ( Figure 6(b) ), echoing the importance of a strong pretrained base model for RL efficiency.

chunks.section: RL amplifies task-relevant skills while preserving unused skills.
chunks.text: We then study how task specification shapes individual skills during fine-tuning. We distinguish useful skills , which contribute to the downstream task, from junk skills , which are present in the base model but unused for finetuned task. As shown in Figure 6(c) , useful skills are further amplified, while junk skills initially deteriorate only mildly and are not catastrophically forgotten. This aligns with previous empirical observations that RL amplifies useful patterns learned during pretraining ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) , and predicts that unused skills may remain largely recoverable for future tasks where they become relevant. (a) Schematic of a compositional RL perceptron where individual skill is modeled as a single RL perceptron and compositional task is defined as a linear combination of those skills. (b) The fine-tuning time required to get the compositional task correct decreases as the pre-trained level of individual skill becomes better. (c) During the finetuning, the skill used in the finetuned compositional task further improves and is amplified. The junk skill previously acquired during pretraining but not used for the compositional task persists, not forgotten. chunks.section: 6 Discussion
chunks.text: Our contribution is an analytically tractable starting point for studying multistage training pipelines in foundation models. Despite its simplicity, the model captures power-law error scaling, SFT–RL complementarity, warm-start dependence, and selective skill amplification. The dependence of downstream learning on pretraining quality is consistent with controlled experiments showing that stronger pretrained models improve faster and reach higher performance under RL ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , and that pretraining quality is a central bottleneck for downstream performance and compute efficiency ( Akter et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . The benefit of supervised preparation is consistent with empirical findings that stronger SFT initialization can improve subsequent RL ( Liu et al., 2025b ) . Our allocation analysis excludes the cost of acquiring high-quality supervision, which can substantially improve post-training ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) but is difficult to obtain at scale. In our model, proportional reductions in label noise yield diminishing absolute improvements in SFT error, while better pretraining reduces sensitivity to noise. Accounting for data acquisition and verification costs could provide more practical insights into when improving supervision is preferable to additional pretraining or RL. Broadly, by making the interactions between pretraining, SFT, and RL analytically tractable, our model provides a starting point for understanding how these stages jointly impact learning performance.

chunks.section: 6 Discussion
chunks.text: Limitations : Our model is a simplified and abstract setup, where each component is modeled as a simple single-layer network. The real-world models rely on complex architectures and heavy engineering, which we do not account for. Our proposed model of RL captures an aspect of bulk feedback in RL, but it assumes independence between all observations in an episode. In practice, the cost of SFT is not just a compute one, but the cost of being able to source enough high quality supervision data we do not take into account the difficulty of obtaining the labels of the data for defining compute budget in our analysis. Using frozen encoder weights is a simplification, in practice all weights are updated during fine-tuning.

chunks.section: .1 Teacher-student framework
chunks.text: There is a growing body of neural network theory of learning and generalization based on a teacher-student framework that applies tools from statistical physics, which allows us to characterize the typical behavior in high-dimensional stochastic systems Gardner and Derrida [1989] , Seung et al. [1992] , Engel [2001] , Bahri et al. [2020] , Zdeborová and Krzakala [2016] . Previous works studied diverse learning paradigms and setups, including vanilla supervised learning Du et al. [2018] , Goldt et al. [2019] , Aubin et al. [2018] , Advani et al. [2020] , continual learning Lee et al. [2021] , Lee et al. [2022] , Asanuma et al. [2021] , curriculum learning Saglietti et al. [2022] , Lee et al. [2024] , transfer learning Gerace et al. [2022] , Lampinen and Ganguli [2018] and online policy learning Patel et al. [2025] .

chunks.section: A.1 Thermodynamic Limit
chunks.text: We follow the standard procedure of Saad and Solla , but the main difference is the random projection which requires averaging over. It was shown by Yoshida and Okada [2019] that macroscopically describing the dynamics when data is sampled from a centred Gaussian generates an infinite hierarchy of order parameters to track, and the ODE system can only be closed if the covariance has a finite number of unique eigenvalues, where there is a pair of order parameters associated to every unique eigenvalue. In our case, the projection onto the empirical principal subspace introduces an effective data covariance with, in general, ρ ​ D \rho D unique eigenvalues. We prevent the infinite cascade of ODEs by approximating the higher-order order parameters in terms of lower order ones using the Hilbert Schmidt Operator projection. We denote by 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{s} and 𝐌 n = 𝐈 − 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{n}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{M}_{s} the orthogonal projectors onto the signal and noise subspaces, respectively. The data covariance is Σ = 𝐌 s + Δ ​ 𝐌 n , \displaystyle\Sigma=\mathbf{M}_{s}+\Delta\mathbf{M}_{n}, (7) where 0 < Δ < 1 0<\Delta<1 . The teacher 𝐰 ∗ \mathbf{w}^{*} is assumed to lie entirely in the signal subspace, so that 𝐌 n ​ 𝐰 ∗ = 0 \mathbf{M}_{n}\mathbf{w}^{*}=0 . The student does not observe 𝐱 \mathbf{x} directly, but instead observes the projected input 𝐏𝐱 \mathbf{P}\mathbf{x} , where 𝐏 \mathbf{P} is the orthogonal projector onto the PCA subspace learned during pretraining. We define the following order parameters:

(23) The coefficients Ω i ​ j ( s ) \Omega_{ij}^{(s)} and Ω i ​ j ( n ) \Omega_{ij}^{(n)} are obtained by Hilbert-Schmidt projection, which we will detail now. The purpose of the Hilbert-Schmidt projection is not to assert that 𝐏𝐌 i ​ 𝐏𝐌 j ​ 𝐏 \mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{i}\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{j}\mathbf{P} is exactly a linear combination of 𝐏𝐌 s ​ 𝐏 \mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{s}\mathbf{P} and 𝐏𝐌 n ​ 𝐏 \mathbf{P}\mathbf{M}_{n}\mathbf{P} . Rather, it gives the unique best approximation to this operator within the space already represented by the order parameters. More precisely, define

The discarded component, or residual operator, is therefore 𝚫 i ​ j = 𝐔 i ​ j − ( Ω i ​ j ( s ) ​ 𝐕 s + Ω i ​ j ( n ) ​ 𝐕 n ) . \displaystyle\mathbf{\Delta}_{ij}=\mathbf{U}_{ij}-(\Omega_{ij}^{(s)}\mathbf{V}_{s}+\Omega_{ij}^{(n)}\mathbf{V}_{n}). This orthogonality does not ensure that the residual contractions with the student and teacher vanish: training can generate correlations with the eigendirections of 𝚫 i ​ j \mathbf{\Delta}_{ij} . Vanishing residual contractions would yield an exact quadratic-form closure, whereas residuals that remain O ⁡ ( 1 ) O(1) require additional macroscopic order parameters. We therefore treat the four-order-parameter dynamics as approximate. Appendix A.6 tests this approximation numerically, finding small relative residuals whose disorder-averaged magnitudes decrease with dimension over the tested range, without establishing self-averaging to zero. chunks.section: B.1 Resolvent representation of the PCA projector
chunks.text: The contour integral is simply a way of replacing the discontinuous operation “keep only eigenvectors in the PCA window” by an analytic operation on the resolvent. Random matrix theory can compute deterministic limits of resolvent traces much more directly than deterministic limits of eigenvector projectors. Thus the problem reduces to evaluating deterministic equivalents for one-, two-, and three-resolvent traces with deterministic insertions 𝐌 s \mathbf{M}_{s} . This is the standard route in random matrix theory for extracting eigenvector information from resolvents; see, for example, Silverstein and Choi [1995] , Ledoit and Péché [2011] . N.B. the contour formula is clean only in the separated case , i.e. where the spectrum is gapped ( γ < 1 \gamma<1 ). If the selected window I I lies inside a connected bulk component, there is no fixed macroscopic contour enclosing the selected eigenvalues and no other spectrum. At finite D D , there is technically a tiny random gap between consecutive eigenvalues, but it vanishes as D → ∞ D\rightarrow\infty . In the gapless quantile-selection regime, the contour picture should be understood as the limiting boundary-value representation obtained by replacing the contour integral by the spectral discontinuity of the resolvent ( 𝐑 Σ ^ ​ ( x + i ​ 0 ) − 𝐑 Σ ^ ​ ( x − i ​ 0 ) \mathbf{R}_{\widehat{\Sigma}}(x+i0)-\mathbf{R}_{\widehat{\Sigma}}(x-i0) ) across the interval I I , we detail this in the subsequent sections. In the Marchenko–Pastur limit, the resolvent traces self-average, so the trace constants can be replaced by their deterministic limits. The purpose of the Matrix Dyson Equation (next section) is to compute these deterministic limits.

Consequently, its resolvent 𝐑 Σ ^ ​ ( z ) = ( Σ ^ − z ​ 𝐈 ) − 1 \displaystyle\mathbf{R}_{\widehat{\Sigma}}(z)=(\widehat{\Sigma}-z\mathbf{I})^{-1} (127) is a nonlinear function of the Gaussian randomness. chunks.section: Appendix G Experimental Details of LAE training
chunks.text: For each batchsize N N 20 LAEs were trained to convergence, the overlap of the projection of the final encoders with the signal subspace was then calculated and averaged over runs. The simple LAE had an encoder 𝐄 ∈ ℝ ( D × K ) \mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{(D\times K)} and a decoder 𝐃 ∈ ℝ ( K × D ) \mathbf{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{(K\times D)} , with D = 2000 D=2000 and K = 400 K=400 . Weights were initialised from zero mean Gaussians with variance 1 / D 1/D and 1 / K 1/K for the encoder and decoder respectively. Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.0001, and 10000 steps were used ensuring convergence. JAX with float32 precision was used.

chunks.section: Appendix H Optimal Compute Allocation Experimental details
chunks.text: In addition to solving the projected ODEs for fixed hyperparameters, we also optimize how a fixed computational budget is allocated between pretraining data selection, SFT updates, and RL updates. The optimization is performed over the deterministic ODE dynamics rather than over stochastic simulations. This makes it possible to evaluate many candidate allocations efficiently. Let B tot B_{\rm tot} denote the total available budget. We allocate this budget between three stages: C P ​ T , C SFT , C RL , C_{PT},\qquad C_{\rm SFT},\qquad C_{\rm RL}, where C P ​ T C_{PT} is the budget spent on choosing the pretraining level α \alpha , C SFT C_{\rm SFT} is the budget spent on SFT updates, and C RL C_{\rm RL} is the budget spent on RL updates. The allocation satisfies C P ​ T + C SFT + C RL = B tot . C_{PT}+C_{\rm SFT}+C_{\rm RL}=B_{\rm tot}. The cost of choosing a pretraining level α \alpha is taken to be linear, C P ​ T = c α ​ α , C_{PT}=c_{\alpha}\alpha, where c α c_{\alpha} is the cost per unit α \alpha . The remaining budget is B ODE ​ ( α ) = B tot − c α ​ α . B_{\rm ODE}(\alpha)=B_{\rm tot}-c_{\alpha}\alpha. For the combined SFT–RL setting, we parameterize the split of this remaining budget by a fraction f SFT ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] f_{\rm SFT}\in[0,1] : C SFT = f SFT ​ B ODE ​ ( α ) , C RL = ( 1 − f SFT ) ​ B ODE ​ ( α ) . C_{\rm SFT}=f_{\rm SFT}B_{\rm ODE}(\alpha),\qquad C_{\rm RL}=(1-f_{\rm SFT})B_{\rm ODE}(\alpha). If the cost per SFT step is a a , and the cost per RL step is b b , then the corresponding numbers of ODE steps are n SFT = C SFT a , n RL = C RL b . n_{\rm SFT}=\frac{C_{\rm SFT}}{a},\qquad n_{\rm RL}=\frac{C_{\rm RL}}{b}.

chunks.section: H.1 Precomputation and interpolation over α \alpha
chunks.text: For each value of α \alpha , the initial condition and closure coefficients are computed from the random-matrix trace constants described in Appendix B . Recomputing these constants at every candidate value of α \alpha would be expensive. We therefore first evaluate them on a fixed interpolation grid α 1 , … , α M , \alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{M}, with M = interp_alpha_res M=\texttt{interp\_alpha\_res} . In the experiments reported here, interp_alpha_res = 200 \texttt{interp\_alpha\_res}=200 unless otherwise stated. For an arbitrary candidate α \alpha , the initial condition ( J s , J n , Q s , Q n ) (J_{s},J_{n},Q_{s},Q_{n}) and the associated constants S , S s , S n , Ω i ​ j ( s ) , Ω i ​ j ( n ) , T s ​ s , T s ​ n , T n ​ n , R S,\quad S_{s},\quad S_{n},\quad\Omega_{ij}^{(s)},\quad\Omega_{ij}^{(n)},\quad T_{ss},\quad T_{sn},\quad T_{nn},\quad R are obtained by linear interpolation between the precomputed values. Here R = Q s + Q n R=Q_{s}+Q_{n} is the projected student norm used when the spherical constraint is imposed. This interpolation step allows the allocation search to vary α \alpha continuously over the search interval while avoiding repeated evaluations of the random-matrix formulas.

chunks.section: H.3 Coarse-to-fine grid search
chunks.text: The budget-allocation problem is solved by a coarse-to-fine grid search. For a given total budget, the largest affordable pretraining level is α max aff = min ⁡ { α max , B tot c α } . \alpha_{\max}^{\rm aff}=\min\left\{\alpha_{\max},\frac{B_{\rm tot}}{c_{\alpha}}\right\}. If α max aff < α min \alpha_{\max}^{\rm aff}<\alpha_{\min} , the budget is declared infeasible. The coarse search evaluates a grid of candidate α \alpha values and SFT fractions: α ∈ { α 1 coarse , … , α N α coarse } , f SFT ∈ { f 1 coarse , … , f N f coarse } . \alpha\in\{\alpha_{1}^{\rm coarse},\ldots,\alpha_{N_{\alpha}}^{\rm coarse}\},\qquad f_{\rm SFT}\in\{f_{1}^{\rm coarse},\ldots,f_{N_{f}}^{\rm coarse}\}. The α \alpha -grid may be linearly spaced or warped according to α ⁡ ( u ) = α min + ( α max aff − α min ) ​ u p , u ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \alpha(u)=\alpha_{\min}+(\alpha_{\max}^{\rm aff}-\alpha_{\min})u^{p},\qquad u\in[0,1], where p = alpha_grid_power p=\texttt{alpha\_grid\_power} . This allows more resolution near small α \alpha when desired. After evaluating the full coarse grid, the algorithm identifies the best top_k coarse α \alpha -regions according to max f SFT ⁡ p gen ​ ( α , f SFT ) . \max_{f_{\rm SFT}}p_{\rm gen}(\alpha,f_{\rm SFT}).

chunks.section: H.3 Coarse-to-fine grid search
chunks.text: Each selected region is then refined. The refined α \alpha -interval is formed by taking a small neighborhood around the selected coarse α \alpha -cell, with width controlled by refine_alpha_half_width_cells . Within each selected region, the algorithm evaluates a finer grid of refine_alpha_res values of α \alpha . The SFT fraction is refined over the full interval f SFT ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] f_{\rm SFT}\in[0,1] , rather than only near the coarse optimum. This is useful because the optimal SFT–RL split can shift substantially as α \alpha changes, especially near the boundary where the remaining ODE budget changes rapidly. The best refined candidate over all selected regions is returned. The reported allocation is ( C P ​ T , C SFT , C RL ) = ( c α ​ α , f SFT ​ B ODE ​ ( α ) , ( 1 − f SFT ) ​ B ODE ​ ( α ) ) , (C_{PT},C_{\rm SFT},C_{\rm RL})=\left(c_{\alpha}\alpha,f_{\rm SFT}B_{\rm ODE}(\alpha),(1-f_{\rm SFT})B_{\rm ODE}(\alpha)\right), together with the corresponding final generalization performance.

chunks.section: H.4 Single-stage baselines
chunks.text: We also evaluate two single-stage baselines. In the SFT-only baseline, f SFT = 1 , C RL = 0 . f_{\rm SFT}=1,\qquad C_{\rm RL}=0. The search is then one-dimensional over α \alpha , and the full remaining ODE budget is spent on SFT: n SFT = B tot − c α ​ α a . n_{\rm SFT}=\frac{B_{\rm tot}-c_{\alpha}\alpha}{a}. In the RL-only baseline, f SFT = 0 , C SFT = 0 , f_{\rm SFT}=0,\qquad C_{\rm SFT}=0, and the remaining budget is spent entirely on RL: n RL = B tot − c α ​ α b . n_{\rm RL}=\frac{B_{\rm tot}-c_{\alpha}\alpha}{b}. Both baselines use the same coarse-to-fine search over α \alpha as the full SFT–RL allocation problem.

chunks.section: H.5 Implementation details
chunks.text: The allocation search is implemented in JAX and run on CPU with 64-bit floating point arithmetic enabled. The ODE update maps for SFT and RL are JIT-compiled. The coarse and refined grids are evaluated using vectorized JAX loops. For each candidate α \alpha , the SFT prefix trajectory is computed once and reused for all candidate values of f SFT f_{\rm SFT} . This reuse is the main computational saving in the two-stage search, because each candidate fraction only requires interpolating along the stored SFT trajectory before running the RL segment. Invalid numerical evaluations, such as candidates producing NaN values, are assigned performance − ∞ -\infty and are therefore excluded from the optimum. For each run, the code saves a JSON file containing the training mode, total budget, task parameters T T and ϵ \epsilon , runtime, maximum ODE step count, best allocation, best performance, selected α \alpha , selected f SFT f_{\rm SFT} , refined search regions, and the full search configuration. The saved search configuration includes the coarse and refined grid resolutions, the number of top coarse regions refined, the α \alpha -grid warping parameter, and the interpolation resolution used for the precomputed random-matrix constants.

chunks.section: Appendix J Details on LLM Experiments
chunks.text: We fine-tuned OLMo-2 1B base model [ OLMo et al., 2024 ] on GSM8K [ Cobbe et al., 2021b ] math word problems across 3 random seeds for each setup. The GSM8K training set was split 90/10 into an RL partition and an SFT partition. In the SFT + RL conditions, the base model was first fine-tuned via supervised learning on the SFT partition (10% of training data, 747 examples) using the full chain-of-thought reasoning traces from GSM8K official dataset for 20, 60, 100, or 300 steps (lr = 2e-4, batch size 8), and the resulting checkpoint was then used to initialize GRPO training. In the RL-only baseline, GRPO training was applied directly to the base model with no SFF a priori. All GRPO runs trained for 1000 steps on the 90% RL partition (lr = 2e-5, batch size 8, 8 generations per prompt, max completion length 768 tokens), using a binary accuracy reward over the GSM8K test format. All models used 4-bit NF4 quantization with LoRA adapters (rank 32) applied to all attention and MLP projection layers. Evaluation reward was computed every 50 steps on a held-out subset of 128 GSM8K test split examples. Both SFT and RL training used the same plain text prompt format applied directly to the base model. Each prompt consisted of a brief instruction: "Solve the math problem. The last line must be exactly: Final answer: boxed ​ { NUMBER } \text{\\ boxed}\{\text{NUMBER}\} ", followed by the problem under a "Problem:" header and a "Solution:" prefix that cued the model to begin its response.

chunks.section: Appendix J Details on LLM Experiments
chunks.text: We used this format to work with a raw base model rather than an instruction-tuned one, providing just enough structure to elicit a parseable answer while keeping the format simple. We verified that before any finetuning, the model can often generate coherent answers with the correct format, but wrong answers. For SFT, the full target sequence was appended. We used the GSM8K dataset’s full answer trace, for example, Natalia sold 48/2 = <<48/2=24>>24 clips in May. Natalia sold 48+24 = <<48+24=72>>72 clips altogether in April and May. followed by the formatted final answer. In this way, we expect the model learned to produce step-by-step solutions ending in the required boxed format. For GRPO, only the prompt portion was provided and the model generated completions freely, with a binary accuracy reward assigned based on whether the final boxed answer matched the ground truth.

chunks.section: Appendix K Compute Resources
chunks.text: Only experiments that required a considerable compute resources was LLM experiment with OlMO 1B model and GSM8k dataset in Figure 3 b. All of the LLM experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. A RL run with our setup took 8 hours, whereas SFT completed in under 1 hour.

chunks.section: Appendix L LLM Usage
chunks.text: We used LLM assistance during manuscript preparation to improve clarity and consistency. In particular, LLMs were used to help reorganize mathematical notation, double-check the presentation of proofs, and improve the manuscript for grammar, style, and readability.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Our abstract summarizes the contribution of our work: a simple analytically tractable model of multi-stage training. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have a dedicated limitation section at the end of the Discussion. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide a theory, its derivation steps and the simulation which directly tests the correctness of the theory. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide the experimental details and hyperparameters used for generating the results. The code for the experiments will be publicly available upon acceptance. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [No] Justification: We provide the experimental details and hyperparameters used for generating the results. The code for the experiments will be publicly available upon acceptance. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We include the details of the hyperparameters for all the results we include in the paper. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Most of our experiment is for the validation of the theory that provides exact learning dynamics. For one experiment with LLM finetuning to compare the characteristics of learning curves, we used 3 seeds and notated mean and standard deviation. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide additional section in appendix for compute resources providing the relevant details for the experiments that required considerable compute. Guidelines:

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We follow the Code of Ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The goal of this work is to advance the theoretical understanding of the foundation model with a complex training pipeline. We do not foresee any direct societal impacts of the work. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A]

chunks.section: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
chunks.text: Justification: N/A Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We used OLMo-2 1B and GSM8K and cited them. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

So far, we have treated pretraining quality as a single scalar controlling the overall usefulness of the learned representation. In practice, however, pretrained models may contain many latent skills, only some of which are relevant to a given downstream task. Fine-tuning on a domain specific task, such as on math or coding, may therefore selectively amplify task-relevant skills rather than uniformly improve the full representation Zhao et al. (2025) ; Shao et al. (2025)
We address this question by extending our analytical model to study RL finetuning as learning to linearly compose multiple ‘pretrained’ skills into a more complex task ( Lee et al., 2024

etely, each skill is represented by one of K K independent teacher-student pairs ( 𝐰 1 ​ … ​ K ∗ , 𝐰 1 ​ … ​ K \mathbf{w}^{*}_{1...K},\mathbf{w}_{1...K} ), and the downstream task is defined by a context teacher-student vector ( V ∗ , V ∈ ℝ K V^{*},V\in\mathbb{R}^{K} ) that selects and combines these skills. During fine-tuning, both the student skills and the context are updated. This setup allows some pretrained skills to be task-relevant, while others are present in the base model but unused by the downstream task. We provide the ODE derivation for this compositional RL setting in Appendix I
